blocks.text: If anyone wishes to know more about this kind of lizard, unknown in these lands, Ibno-saida describes it: دابة علي خلق الضب الا انه اعظم منه [dābba ʿalā khalq al-ḍabb illā annahu aʿẓam minhu] an animal of the nature of the dhab, except that it is larger. And Abdollatif: فاما الورل وهو الحردون [fa-ammā al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥardūn] Guaril is indeed the same as chardaun. But on the contrary Algiahid, in Damir, reports ان الحردون غير الورل ووصفه دابة تكون غالبا بارض مصر موشاة بالوان كثير ولها كف ككف الانسان مقسومة اصابعها الي الانامل [anna al-ḥardūn ghayr al-waral wa-waṣafahu dābba takūn ghāliban bi-arḍ Miṣr muwashshāh bi-alwān kathīr wa-lahā kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūma aṣābiʿuhā ilā al-anāmil] that chardaun is different from guaril; he describes it as an animal common in Egypt, marked with many colours, having hands like those of a man, and fingers divided into joints. And Alkazuinius: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسام ابرص الطويل الذنب الصغير الراس وهو سريع السير خفيف الحركة [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sāmm abraṣ al-ṭawīl al-dhanab al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs wa-huwa sarīʿ al-sayr khafīf al-ḥaraka] It is the largest of the lizards that have the form of the guezga and the sam-mabras (these are species of stellio, the former smaller, the latter larger), with a long tail, a small head, a swift gait and nimble movement. Avicenna too, after comparing it with the stellios and describing its tail and head in the same way as Alkazuinius, says: وهو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف الورل وربما قاربة في طبايعه [wa-huwa ghayr al-ḍabb wa-al-ḍabb lā yakūn aw qall mā yakūn illā fī al-bādiya wa-raʾsuhu wa-badanuhu wa-dhanabuhu khālaf al-waral wa-rubbamā qārabahu fī ṭabāʾiʿihi] And it is different from the dhab (or land crocodile).

[II, 496] For the dhab is never, or very rarely, found anywhere but in the desert. And in head, body and tail it differs from the guaril. Yet it is close to it in nature. Hence Alcamus: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ طويل الذنب صغير الراس [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh ṭawīl al-dhanab ṣaghīr al-raʾs] Guaril is an animal like the dhab, large among those which have the form of the guezga, with a long tail and a small head. Some think it is born from the seed of the crocodile, like the skink; but Damir refutes them, both because they differ much in skin and hide, and because their size is very unequal: والورل لا يزيد قدره علي ذراعين او ذراع ونصف والتمساح عشرة [col. 1072] اذرع واكثر [wa-al-waral lā yazīd qadruhu ʿalā dhirāʿayn aw dhirāʿ wa-niṣf wa-al-timsāḥ ʿashara adhruʿ wa-akthar] For the guaril does not grow beyond two cubits, or one and a half, whereas the crocodile grows beyond ten cubits and more. The same animal is described as very lustful. Abdollatif: فليس في الحيوان اكثر سفاد منه [fa-laysa fī al-ḥayawān akthar sifādan minhu] There is no animal that copulates more often. And, if Alcamus is to be believed, شحمه يعظم الذكر دلكا [shaḥmuhu yuʿaẓẓim al-dhakar dalkan]. Let him understand this who can. He says the same about eating its flesh: لحمه حار جدا يسمن بقوة [laḥmuhu ḥārr jiddan yusamminu bi-quwwa] Its flesh is very hot and fattens greatly. And Alkazuinius: لحمه وشحمه سمن طبقات الناس [laḥmuhu wa-shaḥmuhu samman ṭabaqāt al-nās] Its flesh and fat fatten women above all. So also Avicenna and Damir. They add that the same flesh has a power by which it draws out of the body السلي والشوك [al-salā wa-al-shawk] splinters and thorns; that its hairs, tied to a woman's arm, prevent conception; that numb limbs are revived if smeared with the ash of its burnt skin mixed with the dregs of oil; that its dung removes white spots of the eye, freckles and warts; and finally that its blood strengthens and sharpens the sight. They write the same of the land crocodile.

It may be asked whether this lizard is the same as the green lizard, which many things will seem to suggest. 1. The green lizard is the largest of those found among us. Erasmus in the Dialogue On Friendship: Italy has large lizards, and green ones. Gesner: They are almost twice as large as common lizards. 2. Green lizards are ὀφιομάχοι [ophiomachoi]. Erasmus in the same place: This animal is by nature both friendly to man and hostile to serpents. And a little later: One day I saw a very large and wonderfully green one fighting with a serpent at the mouth of a hole. At first we wondered what was going on, for the serpent was not visible to us. An Italian told us that the enemy was in the cave. A little later the lizard came to us, as if showing its wounds and begging for a remedy, etc. The serpent had gnawed away almost the whole of one side and had turned it from green to red. So what we read in Pliny, that lizards fight with serpents, should be referred to these lizards. Hence the more recent writers gave it the name ὀφιονίκος [ophionikos].

[II, 497] The Pandectarius: OFIONICOS in Greek, that is, lizard. 3. Just as the Arabs write that they grow fat by eating the guaril, so Pliny and Marcellus report that the green lizard is most useful for consumptives and benefits them incredibly. 4. The dung of both, smeared on the face, is said to remove blemishes. Yet colour distinguishes the guaril from the green lizard, for Algiahid describes it as variegated. Moreover the guaril, as the Arabs describe it, seems far to surpass the green lizard in strength and fierceness of spirit. I therefore think that the guaril is a kind of lizard peculiar to Arabia, and that the green lizard is so similar to it that it is
Next to it, but next by a long interval.
